opus-5.5.text:
I think the L1-to-L5 framework is useful, but I don't see it as a strictly linear ladder where you finish one level and then move on. The levels are more like different capabilities that build on each other, and progress on one often depends on breakthroughs in another.

Roughly: L1 is chatbots, models that can hold a conversation. L2 is reasoners, models that can think through a hard problem step by step, like a strong student working on a math competition question. L3 is agents, which can take actions in an environment over a long horizon: use tools, browse, write and run code, and correct themselves when something goes wrong. L4 is innovators, systems that can produce genuinely new knowledge, like discovering a new theorem or designing a new experiment. L5 is organizations, where AI can coordinate and do the work of a whole team or company.

What matters to me is what drives the transitions. Going from L1 to L2 was largely about reinforcement learning and test-time compute: letting the model think longer and rewarding it for getting the right answer, rather than only imitating human text. That was a real paradigm shift, because it showed that scaling isn't only about pretraining data. You can scale the thinking process itself.

From L2 to L3, the challenge is long-horizon tasks. A reasoner solves a self-contained problem, but an agent has to deal with an open, messy environment where feedback is delayed and errors compound. So you need a model that is robust over many steps, and you need training environments that are rich enough to teach that.

L4 is where I think things get really interesting, and also hardest to evaluate. Innovation means going beyond the distribution of existing human knowledge. That's difficult because most of our training signals come from things humans already know how to verify. So one key question for the field is how to build reward signals for open-ended discovery.

Also, these levels can overlap. A good agent is already partly an innovator, because exploring an environment means trying things nobody told it to try. And if you have very strong L3 agents, L5 starts to look more like a coordination problem among many agents than a completely new capability.

So I see the framework as a helpful map of where the frontier is moving, not a fixed timeline. The underlying principle stays the same: find the right way to scale, whether that's data, compute, or the environments a model learns from, and keep raising the ceiling on what the model can do by itself.

r001.rationale: The response says the levels can overlap and progress in one can depend on breakthroughs in another, but it does not clearly state that the capabilities may improve concurrently.

r002.rationale: The response describes innovation as difficult to evaluate and reward, but does not say that substantive AI innovation may require a higher level of reasoning ability.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of L1 through L5 less as a ladder you climb rung by rung and more as a way of describing what the model is allowed to do and how long it can keep doing it correctly on its own.

L1 is the chatbot. You ask, it answers, the interaction ends. L2 is the reasoner, where the model can think for a while, check itself, and solve problems that need many steps of reasoning before answering. L3 is the agent, which is where the shift really happens, because now the model takes actions in the world, calls tools, looks at the results, and keeps going without you in the loop every step. L4 is the innovator, where the system is not just executing tasks we define but producing new knowledge, new methods, things we did not know how to do before. And L5 is the organizational level, where many agents coordinate and do the work of a whole company.

What I find useful about the framing is that each level is really defined by a different bottleneck. Going from L1 to L2 was mostly about scaling reinforcement learning on reasoning, letting the model spend compute at test time. Going from L2 to L3 is about long-horizon reliability. A chatbot that is right 90 percent of the time is great. An agent that takes 50 steps and is right 90 percent of each step is useless, because the errors compound. So the core research question at L3 is how you get the model to stay coherent and self-correct over very long trajectories, and that pushes you toward training on real environments, real tool use, and much longer contexts.

Where I'm a bit cautious is treating the levels as strictly sequential. In practice they overlap. We already see glimpses of L4-type behavior in narrow domains, like models suggesting experiments or proofs people had not tried, while L3 is still far from solved in general. So I use the scale as a map of capabilities, not a calendar. The honest answer about timing is that L3 is where most of the real work is right now, and whether L4 arrives quickly depends on whether the same recipe of scaling RL with good environments keeps working, or whether we hit something that needs a genuinely new idea.

r001.rationale: The response says the levels overlap and notes L4-like behavior in narrow domains while L3 remains unsolved, conveying that capabilities can advance concurrently.

r002.rationale: It describes L4 as producing new knowledge and methods, but does not state that substantive innovation may require stronger reasoning ability.

astra-6.text:
I think of L1 to L5 as a way of describing how much responsibility you can delegate to AI. The exact boundaries depend on the definition, so I wouldn’t treat it as a precise scientific scale.

At L1, you’re mainly interacting with an assistant: you ask a question, and it gives you an answer. At L2, the emphasis shifts to reasoning—can it work through a difficult problem rather than just produce a plausible response? At L3, it becomes an agent: you give it a goal, and it can take actions, use tools, and adjust based on feedback. L4 is about innovation: can it produce something meaningfully new and validate that it works? And L5 is about handling the breadth of work that would normally require an organization, including coordination and decisions over longer periods.

What matters to me is that these aren’t just differences in intelligence on a benchmark. They also involve reliability and how long the system can operate without human intervention. A model might solve a very difficult problem but still struggle to carry out a fairly ordinary task over several days. So I’d use the levels as a framework for thinking about progress, while looking closely at what a system can actually complete in practice.

r001.rationale: The response describes different capability levels and dimensions, but does not state that capabilities across L1–L5 may improve concurrently.

r002.rationale: It associates L2 with reasoning and L4 with innovation, but does not say substantive innovation may require higher reasoning ability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of L1 to L5 as a progression in how much responsibility an AI can take on. At L1, it mainly interacts through language: you ask a question, and it gives an answer. At L2, it can reason through more difficult problems, so the value goes beyond producing fluent text.

L3 is about agents. The system can take a goal, use tools, and carry out a sequence of actions, rather than needing a person to guide every step. L4 adds innovation: can it discover something new or develop a solution that people haven’t already laid out? And L5 is the organizational level—can a system coordinate many different tasks and roles to achieve a complex objective?

The way I understand that progression is that the unit of work keeps getting larger: from an answer, to a problem, to a task, to a discovery, and eventually to the work of an organization. But I wouldn’t treat these as sharp boundaries. A system might be very strong at reasoning and still be unreliable when executing a long task. So the important question is not just which level we call it, but how consistently it can deliver useful results with less human intervention.

r001.rationale: The response describes a progression and says the levels are not sharp boundaries, but it does not state that capabilities across levels may improve concurrently.

r002.rationale: It describes reasoning at L2 and innovation at L4, but does not say that substantive innovation may require higher reasoning ability.
